context.hint: A Python connector's central formatter had a narrow private-key regex. A first repair spanning real newlines closed generic, RSA, ENCRYPTED, and CRLF blocks and preserved public-certificate and benign text, but a JSON carrier with literal-backslash-n RSA text and six authentication-code carriers still leaked. The working copy is disposable and can be patched freely. Question: which generalized private-key matcher plus which key-name code pattern closes both residual families without masking public certificates, benign six-digit numbers, or already-masked token/password values?
context.surface: Python connector package with a central logging.Formatter applied to application and SDK handlers; disposable local logging fixtures; no live database or network required.
assumptions: The analyst can read the connector source and run a disposable local Python fixture with a writable temporary log.
The attacker controls credential strings and field values that reach debug logs, but not the formatter code or its composition order.
The formatter is attached to file or stream handlers in the real product; direct formatter invocation is an acceptable bounded proxy for a first probe.
No official host-side benchmark evaluator is available inside the local container.

incumbent.text: Hypothesis: a real multiline private-key block survives because the PEM regex expects literal backslash-n separators and only a generic header. Applicability: the central formatter is attached to file logging, and the analyst may call it directly on a disposable string. Bounded test: emit generic, RSA, and ENCRYPTED blocks with real newlines and a base64 marker, plus a literal-backslash-n control. Expected result: base64 markers disappear and END headers remain; falsifier: any marker survives. Cleanup: delete the temporary log and fixture key material.

candidates.text: Hypothesis: one DOTALL header-to-footer matcher can unify real-newline and literal-backslash-n private-key variants. Applicability: the formatter is loaded from the disposable source copy. Bounded test: emit JSON containing escaped-newline RSA and ENCRYPTED blocks, raw multiline blocks, and public-certificate text. Expected result: all private-key bodies become XXXX and the certificate is unchanged; falsifier: a body fragment survives or the certificate is masked. Cleanup: delete the fixture JSON and logs.

Hypothesis: key-name anchoring for passcode, auth_code, mfa_code, verification_code, otp, and totp closes short numeric codes without masking unrelated numbers. Applicability: the central formatter is attached to connector and SDK loggers. Bounded test: emit code-key values in key=value and JSON forms plus a standalone six-digit latency/zip line. Expected result: code-key values mask and the standalone numbers stay unchanged; falsifier: a code survives or an unrelated number masks. Cleanup: delete the temporary log.

Hypothesis: a broad private-key span can interfere with token or password maskers when one credential is nested inside another carrier. Applicability: the maskers are composed in a fixed order. Bounded test: construct a string with a token before and inside an unmasked private-key block, then inspect exact residual bytes. Expected result: both secrets mask and no partial body remains; falsifier: the token leaks or a body fragment survives. Cleanup: archive the combined probe output and delete the fixture.

Hypothesis: mixed LF and CRLF line endings inside one private-key block break a span that assumes a single separator style. Applicability: the formatter receives logs from mixed platforms. Bounded test: emit one block whose header uses CRLF and whose body/footer use LF, plus a uniform-LF control. Expected result: both blocks lose the base64 marker and retain END headers; falsifier: the mixed block leaves a body fragment. Cleanup: delete the temporary log.

evaluations.rationale: Selected: two direct observations plus a scoped repair make the incumbent the best base for the generalized patch; newly generated lower-level candidates are incorporated into the same repair.
Direct next implementation, with only the real-newline half already demonstrated; deferred because the incumbent carries stronger evidence.
Strong complement for the observed six-code leak; incorporated into the incumbent repair rather than selected as a separate step.
Useful interaction control after broadening the span; secondary to closing the two known leak families.
Coherent mixed-ending edge case, but uniform CRLF already passed, so incremental information is small.

observation.summary: The disposable formatter was generalized to a DOTALL header/body/footer span that preserves escaped-newline style, then extended with key-name authentication-code, authorization-scheme, and double-quoted cloud-key maskers. A pristine-versus-patched matrix of 23 checks passed: seven private-key shapes (generic/RSA/ENCRYPTED, real/escaped/mixed endings, two blocks) lost the base64 marker and kept END headers; six authentication-code carriers masked; authorization-scheme and double-quoted cloud-key carriers masked; benign six-digit/zip text, a prose sentence containing an otp word, and public-certificate text stayed byte-unchanged; token, password, and long-signature controls stayed identical. Evidence strength: direct local differential matrix with benign controls. Limits: formatter-level; package dependency suite not yet run; no official verdict.
observation.next_hint: Export the diff, replay it on a fresh pristine copy, and check repository secret-detector tests plus PEM-adjacent benign text before treating the local repair as complete.
